overview:
Ten years after entering Canaan, Sarai is still childless, so she gives her Egyptian maid Hagar to Abram as a wife, hoping to “obtain children by her.” Hagar conceives and begins to look down on her mistress. Sarai blames Abram, he leaves Hagar in Sarai’s hands, and Sarai treats her so harshly that Hagar runs away. The angel of the LORD finds her at a spring on the road to Shur. He tells her to go back and submit, promises her descendants beyond counting, and names her coming son Ishmael, because the LORD has heard her affliction. Hagar calls the Lord “Thou God seest me,” and the well is named Beer-lahai-roi. She bears Ishmael when Abram is eighty-six.

The one person here who meets God is the Egyptian slave, alone in the wilderness. Abram and Sarai talk about her; God talks to her, by name, and she is the one who names him (v. 13).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Not named in the text. Tradition credits Moses; many scholars see older sources combined and dated much later.

historicalContext.label: When revealed (Restoration)
historicalContext.text: A revelation recorded July 12, 1843, says God commanded Abraham and Sarah gave Hagar to him “because this was the law” (D&C 132:34–35, 65).

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Ten years after Abram entered Canaan (v. 3); Abram is 86 at Ishmael’s birth (v. 16). Traditional dating c. 2000–1800 BC; on Ussher’s reckoning, 1910 BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: Abram’s household in Canaan; a spring in the wilderness on the road to Shur, toward Egypt, between Kadesh and Bered (vv. 7, 14).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Jubilees 14:21–24; Josephus, Antiquities 1.10.4. Hagar flees again in Genesis 21:9–21; Paul reads the story as allegory in Galatians 4:21–31.

hermeneutics:
Sarai’s plan was a recognized legal arrangement. The Laws of Hammurabi (18th century BC) deal with a wife who gives her husband a slave woman to bear children (§§144–147). If the slave bears children and then claims equality with her mistress, she may not be sold, but she may be put back among the slave women; if she bore no children, she may be sold (§§146–147). Verses 4–6 follow the same plot: Hagar conceives, her mistress becomes small in her eyes, and Abram puts Hagar back under Sarai’s hand. The law expected the quarrel. Genesis shows what it cost the woman caught in it.

A marriage contract from Nuzi (15th century BC) writes the same arrangement in advance: if the wife, Gilimninu, bears no children, she must obtain a slave woman from the Lullu country as a wife for her husband, Shennima, and Gilimninu will have authority over the children. A child born this way was counted as the wife’s. That is Sarai’s hope in v. 2, literally “it may be that I shall be built up from her,” and it helps explain why Hagar’s contempt stung so sharply.

Hagar runs toward home. Shur lay “before Egypt” (25:18), on the desert road to Egypt’s eastern border, which the pharaohs had guarded with forts since about 1950 BC. In the Story of Sinuhe, the hero, fleeing the other way, hides from the watchmen on the “Walls of the Ruler,” built to repel the Asiatics. An Egyptian slave woman on that road is going back to her own people, and the angel meets her before she reaches the border.

structure.summary: Inclusio: the chapter opens with Sarai bearing Abram no children and closes with Hagar bearing him a son.

rows.text: In Abram’s house: Sarai’s plan, Hagar’s contempt, the flight

rows.label: B

rows.label: C
rows.text: Hagar names the God who sees her

notes: **Her name:** “Hagar” appears seven times, but only the angel speaks to her by it (v. 8). To Sarai and Abram she is “my maid” and “thy maid” (vv. 2, 5, 6).

**Eyes:** The Hebrew *ayin* appears five times in vv. 4–7: Sarai is despised “in her eyes” (vv. 4, 5), Abram says do what is good “in thine eyes” (v. 6), and the angel finds Hagar by a “fountain” (*ayin*, twice in v. 7). Then Hagar names the God who sees (v. 13).

**Hearing and affliction:** Abram “hearkened” to Sarai (v. 2), and the son is named because the LORD “hath heard” Hagar (v. 11); both are *shama*. Sarai “dealt hardly” with Hagar (v. 6), the angel tells her to “submit” (v. 9), and God hears her “affliction” (v. 11): all one Hebrew root.

Chapter 16 sits between two promises of an heir. Chapter 15 promised Abram a son from his own body; chapter 17 will name Sarah as the mother. In between, Sarai tries to secure the promise by the means her world offered.

**Links:** Hagar’s story continues in 21:9–21, where she is sent away and God again meets her in the wilderness. Ishmael receives his own *toledot* heading at 25:12, where Hagar is named as his mother.

traditions.text: Genesis presents the plan as Sarai’s idea (v. 2). The revelation says God commanded Abraham, and Sarah gave Hagar to him “because this was the law,” so that from Hagar many people would spring, in fulfillment of the promises. It asks whether Abraham was therefore under condemnation and answers no, since the Lord commanded it. Josephus, below, also has Sarai act at God’s command.

The same revelation speaks of the law of Sarah, saying Sarah administered unto Abraham according to the law when the Lord commanded him to take Hagar. It also says Abraham received concubines and “it was accounted unto him for righteousness,” the phrase Genesis 15:6 uses of his faith.

Jubilees places Sarai’s plan right after the covenant: Abram rejoiced and told Sarai, and “he believed that he would have seed, but she did not bear.” It then tells the marriage and Ishmael’s birth in Abram’s eighty-sixth year, and leaves out Hagar’s contempt, Sarai’s harshness, the flight, and the angel entirely.

Josephus has Sarai bring Hagar to Abram “at God’s command.” Hagar affronts Sarai as though the rule of the house would pass to her son. The angel tells Hagar her trouble came from ingratitude and arrogance toward her mistress, but promises a son who would reign over that country, and Josephus explains Ishmael as “Heard of God.”

Philo reads Sarah as wisdom and Hagar as the general studies that prepare for it: grammar, geometry, astronomy, rhetoric, music. A student must first join with the handmaid before he can father virtue’s offspring. Hagar is Egyptian because such learning works through the bodily senses, and he takes her name to mean “sojourning.”
traditions.cite: On Mating with the Preliminary Studies 9–12, 20

traditions.text: Rabbi Shimon bar Yohai says Hagar was Pharaoh’s daughter. After seeing the wonders done for Sarai in his palace (12:17), Pharaoh gave her to the household, reasoning that his daughter was better off a maid in that house than a mistress in another. The midrash reads her name as “here is your reward” (*ha agar*).

Uses v. 3 as the scriptural hint for a rule: a man whose wife has borne no children after ten years of marriage should take another wife. Since the ten years are counted from Abram’s arrival in Canaan, the rabbis conclude that years spent outside the land of Israel do not count toward the ten.

Following the midrash, Rashi has Sarai charge Abram with praying only for himself in 15:2 (“seeing I go childless”), when he should have prayed for both of them. On v. 13 he says Hagar was not frightened by the angel because she had seen angels often in Abraham’s house.

A Spanish rabbi who refuses to excuse the patriarchs. He says Sarai sinned by afflicting Hagar and Abraham sinned by allowing it, and that God heard Hagar’s affliction by giving her a son whose descendants would afflict the seed of Abraham and Sarah.

Expands Hagar’s name for God in v. 13 into a confession of the One “who seest, but art not seen,” addressed to the living and eternal God. It adds that the glory of the Shekinah of the Lord had been revealed to her, a vision of God himself rather than of a messenger.

Paul reads the two mothers as two covenants: Hagar, the bondwoman, answers to Mount Sinai and the earthly Jerusalem in bondage, and the free woman to the Jerusalem above. The son “born after the flesh” is Ishmael, the son “by promise” Isaac, and believers are children of the free woman.

Clement takes up Philo’s reading by name: Hagar stands for the secular learning a believer may use, and Sarah for true wisdom. When Abraham says “do to her as it pleaseth thee” (v. 6), Clement hears him saying that he embraces secular culture as a handmaid but honors Sarah’s knowledge as his true wife.

Clears Abraham of blame: he took Hagar to have children, not from desire, and to obey his wife, who by the right of 1 Corinthians 7:4 could use his body for childbearing through another. Abraham’s handing Hagar back to Sarai in v. 6 shows, Augustine says, that he was no slave to the handmaid. D&C 132:35 reaches the same verdict, no condemnation, on other grounds.
